slides.text: In the conservatory glasshouse at Kew, there is a climbing desert cactus called the Queen of the Night that blooms only once every seven years, opening its white petals at midnight and wilting before sunrise. After my divorce, I took the night-watchman job just to walk among the warm tropical ferns while the rest of London froze outside.

Dr. Clara Lin, the head botanist, stayed late every evening with a notebook and a thermos of ginger tea, measuring the tiny green bud on the cactus. She was fiercely guarded, convinced that every good thing in life was fleeting. 'Why love something that takes seven years to arrive and dies in four hours?' she asked me one frosty night, her glasses fogging in the humid air.

In late January, at 1:10 AM, the bud finally trembled and unfurled into a breathtaking crown of ivory petals, flooding the glasshouse with the scent of vanilla and starlight. Clara didn't look at the flower. She was looking at me as I wrapped my wool coat around her shoulders, her fingers lacing tightly through mine. 'Maybe,' she whispered against my collarbone, 'four hours is enough to change the next seven years.'
